Question: Why are some quantities represented as positive and others as negative? Is there a reason for this distinction, and what would happen if all quantities were only given as positive numbers?
Answer: Signed quantities are used when the quantity can go in two opposite directions: up and down, hot and cold, profit and loss, income and expense and so on. This allows quantities to be combined in a meaningful way. If I earned 100 dollars and spent 30 dollars my net income is +100+(–30) = +70 dollars. If all quantities were given as positive numbers in cases where they can go in two opposite directions we would have to always specify the direction, and have rules for handling quantities with the direction specified. So when two quantities with the same direction were combined we would know to add them and give the result the same direction as the two quantities. And when two quantities with opposite directions were combined we would know to subtract the smaller from the larger and give the result the direction of the larger. Using positive and negative allows us to handle all such situations uniformly and not have to have separate rules for each situation where quantities have one of two opposite directions.

Question: What is the method for finding the exact value of a square root with decimals without a calculator?
Answer: There may not be a decimal representation of the exact value of a square root - many square roots are irrational and their decimal representation consists of a non-repeating sequence of digits. But we can use the following method to calculate a square root to any desired degree of precision: Make an initial guess of the square root. Iteratively calculate a new guess as the average of the previous guess and the number divided by the previous guess. The guesses will converge on the square root of the number. Stop when either the guess repeats, in which case we have the exact square root, or when the guess is as precise as we want, in which case it is the square root to the desired degree of precision.
